To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the majority of agricultural waste is used as feed and fuel; (ii) farmers with different livelihood strategy allocate agricultural waste differently to soil amendment; (iii) farmers who use compost have more positive nutrient balances; (iv) farmers demand for compost is affected by farm characteristics and the availability of labour.
the utilisation of agricultural wastes for soil amendment is low and that the main cause is competition for fuel and feed.

(1) the use of agricultural waste as soil amendment is limited due to competition between fuel and feed, and (2) the use of urban waste compost for soil amendment is promising, but its use is limited to educated, large-scale farmers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the utilisation of agricultural wastes for soil amendment and demand for compost.
the use of agricultural waste and urban waste compost as alternatives for chemical fertilisers.
the use of agricultural waste as alternative option for fuel and feed and the use of urban waste compost to improve soil fertility.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the utilisation of agricultural wastes is low and that the demand for compost is high.
the use of agricultural wastes as soil amendments in developing countries is limited due to the lack of knowledge and the competition of fuel and feed.
the use of urban waste compost is not only an option for soil amendment, but is also a promising alternative for the utilisation of agricultural wastes in Ethiopia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
farmers in developing countries should be encouraged to allocate agricultural waste to soil improvement.
agricultural waste utilisation strategies vary between farmers and that urban waste compost is a viable option to improve nutrient balances of smallholder farms.
agricultural waste utilisation for soil amendment should be improved by replacing feed and fuel with sustainable means.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of agricultural waste and urban waste compost for soil fertility management is a viable alternative to inorganic fertilisers, especially for resource-poor farmers.
the allocation of agricultural waste between feed and fuel is the major obstacle for the use of agricultural waste as a soil amendment.
agricultural waste utilisation strategies vary among farmers and are linked to nutrient balances of their farming systems.
